subject: Critical Thinking
title: Amphiboly: Grammatical Ambiguity as a Weapon
description: A fast breakdown of Amphiboly: Grammatical Ambiguity as a Weapon for builders.

hook.text: 'The professor said on Monday he would give the exam.' Did he say it on Monday, or is the exam on Monday?

buildup.text: Amphiboly: a fallacy where grammatical ambiguity allows a sentence to be interpreted in multiple contradictory ways.

discovery.text: The Oracle at Delphi used it masterfully: 'A great empire will be destroyed' – the king assumed it meant the enemy's.

twist.text: Legal contracts are carefully drafted to avoid amphiboly. A misplaced comma once cost a Canadian company $2 million.

climax.text: In arguments, amphiboly lets people claim they meant the other interpretation — a built-in escape hatch.

punchline.text: If a sentence can mean two things, assume the speaker will pick whichever helps.

quiz.question: What is amphiboly?
options: Grammatical ambiguity allowing multiple contradictory interpretations

details.summary: Amphiboly exploits grammatical ambiguity to create misleading arguments. A sentence structure allows two readings, and the arguer uses whichever interpretation serves their purpose, switching between them as needed.
details.whyItMatters: Legal contracts, political promises, and advertising frequently use amphiboly to create statements that can be interpreted in opposing ways depending on convenience.
takeaways: Grammatical structure creates the ambiguity, not word meaning
Amphiboly differs from equivocation, which shifts word meaning
Careful sentence parsing reveals the two possible readings

faq.question: What is a simple example of amphiboly in everyday language?
faq.answer: A sign reading 'Visitors who can read English must translate for those who cannot' — it is unclear whether visitors are being asked to help or whether only literate visitors are allowed. The grammar permits both interpretations.

faq.question: How does amphiboly differ from equivocation?
faq.answer: Equivocation uses a word with two different meanings. Amphiboly uses a sentence structure that can be parsed in two ways. The ambiguity is grammatical rather than semantic. Both exploit ambiguity but at different linguistic levels.
